This isn't a scene from a film. This is a heartbreaking reality that still exists in parts of Nepal. For some women and girls, getting their period means being sent away from their own home to spend the night in a small shed, away from their families. They are left to face cold nights, fear, loneliness, and the danger of snakes, insects, and wild animals—all because of a natural biological process. Menstruation should never be a reason for exclusion or shame. Take a moment and ask yourself: If it were someone you love—your daughter, your sister, your wife, or your mother—would you accept this as "tradition"? Some customs deserve to be questioned, especially when they put lives and dignity at risk. Every woman deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued, no matter what day of the month it is. Let's raise awareness, start conversations, and stand together to end harmful practices like this. November 14, 2026 Gorkha District, Nepal A large dry landslide occurred in Gorkha District. A mass of earth and rock collapsed from the Gundrung Pakha slope into the Thado Bharyang forest area near Yarubagar. Rocks began falling as early as Friday night, and the main landslide took place around 8:30 a.m., kicking up a massive cloud of dust. Debris reached the Budhi Gandaki River. The landslide blocked both a motorable road and a foot trail. According to the district police, there were no casualties or material damage.

The situation in Nepal remains devastating. The amount of mud and debris is overwhelming, and the work is challenging. But our team continues working alongside the local communities, doing everything we can to salvage as many belongings as possible from the rubble and disinfect homes to make them safe again. Sunita is one of the many homeowners our team has met along the way. She remains in her home, carefully cleaning, salvaging what is valuable to her, and gathering the belongings she hopes to recover. Every item saved is a little piece of her life and memories preserved. We’re still here doing our best to support as many families as possible.

After devastating floods washed away a bridge in Nepal, families on the other side were cut off from the people and help they count on. To reach them, Kriti and Binod, communicators with World Vision Nepal, crossed the floodwaters by zipline! Reaching families is where relief begins. Across communities affected by disasters, our teams listen to what families need, help their stories reach the wider world, and work to get emergency supplies where it’s needed most.
